lead: A parabolic reflector, the dish, takes the spherical wave spreading from a small feed at its focus and sends it out as a plane wave across its whole mouth. A plane wave over an aperture many wavelengths wide gives very high gain and a very narrow beam: a 3 m dish at 4 GHz gives about 40 dBi with a beam under 2° wide. Dishes carry satellite TV, radar, deep-space links and microwave hops between towers. The design questions are where to put the feed, how strongly to light the rim, and how much gain and beamwidth result.
prereq: You need: effective aperture and aperture efficiency from aperture and horn antennas, and gain and beamwidth from the antenna fundamentals topic.

sections.h3: Why a parabola makes a plane wave

blocks.text: A parabola is the set of points equally far from a fixed point, the focus, and a fixed line, the directrix. Turn it about its axis and you get a paraboloid. With the vertex at the origin and the axis along z, the surface is z = r²/(4f), where r is the distance from the axis and f the focal length, the distance from the vertex to the focus. A dish of diameter D has its rim at r = D/2.

Every ray from the focus reflects parallel to the axis, and every such ray travels the same total distance from the focus to any plane across the mouth. All of them arrive in phase, so the spherical front from the feed becomes a plane front of width D. By reciprocity the dish works the same way on receive, collecting a plane wave into the feed.

blocks.where: ψ<sub>0</sub> is the half angle the rim subtends at the focus: the feed must light ±ψ<sub>0</sub>. Small f/D (a deep dish) means a wide ψ<sub>0</sub>; f/D is usually 0.25 to 0.5.

blocks.text: Prime focus: a horn at the focus looks back at the dish. It is simple, but the feed, its cable and its struts sit in front of the aperture and block part of it. Cassegrain: a small hyperbolic subreflector placed between the vertex and the focus sends the beam back through a hole at the vertex to a feed behind the dish, so the receiver sits close to the feed with a short, low-loss line; only the subreflector shadows the centre. Gregorian: a concave ellipsoidal subreflector placed beyond the focus does the same job. An offset dish, the kind on most DTH roofs, uses only one side of a paraboloid so that the feed is out of the beam altogether.

The feed’s own pattern decides how the dish is lit. Power aimed past the rim is spillover: it is lost and, on receive, picks up warm ground noise. A feed that lights the rim weakly cuts spillover but wastes the outer part of the dish (taper loss). The best compromise lights the rim about 10 dB below the centre. Blockage, cross-polarization and surface error take more: Ruze’s rule says a surface with RMS error ε loses the factor e−(4πε/λ)², so ε = λ/16 already costs 2.7 dB and ε = λ/30 costs 0.8 dB. Practical dishes reach an overall η = 0.55 to 0.7.

blocks.where: G is the gain as a ratio; η is the aperture efficiency; D is the diameter and λ the wavelength in the same unit. It is the aperture formula G = 4πA<sub>e</sub>/λ² with A<sub>e</sub> = η πD²/4.
HPBW is the half-power beamwidth and BWFN the beamwidth between first nulls, in degrees. 70λ/D suits the usual tapered feed; a uniformly lit circular aperture gives 58λ/D for the half-power width.

blocks.text: Two scaling facts follow. The same dish at twice the frequency has four times the gain (+6 dB) and half the beamwidth, until the surface error becomes a sizeable fraction of λ. And (πD/λ)² equals 4π times the mouth area counted in square wavelengths, which is the aperture formula again, not the number of square wavelengths itself.

examples.question: A 3 m dish works at 4 GHz with aperture efficiency 0.6. Find the gain in dBi, the half-power beamwidth and the beamwidth between first nulls.
steps: Cross-check with the area form: A<sub>e</sub> = 0.6 × π × 3²/4 = 4.241 m²; 4π × 4.241/0.075² = 9475.
examples.answer: G ≈ 9475, that is 39.8 dBi; HPBW about 1.75° and BWFN about 3.5°. A pointing error of 0.9°, half the beamwidth, would already cost 3 dB.

examples.question: The same 3 m dish has f/D = 0.4. Find the focal length, the depth of the dish at its rim, and the angle the feed must illuminate.
steps: f = 0.4 × 3 = 1.2 m in front of the vertex.
Rim radius r = 1.5 m; depth z = r²/(4f) = 2.25/4.8 = 0.469 m.

ψ<sub>0</sub> = 64° is less than 90°, so the focus lies outside the mouth plane: f = 1.2 m is more than the depth 0.469 m. The feed is easy to mount, but the edges of its beam must be kept off the rim to limit spillover.
examples.answer: f = 1.2 m, depth 0.47 m, and the feed must cover ±64° from the axis, putting its −10 dB edge near the rim.

traps: Drawing the feed on the dish. The prime-focus feed sits at the focus, a distance f in front of the vertex.
Dropping η or the π. G = η(πD/λ)²: leaving out η = 0.6 adds 2.2 dB; writing (D/λ)² instead of (πD/λ)² is wrong by π², nearly 10 dB.
Mixing units in 70λ/D. λ and D must be in the same unit; the answer is in degrees.
Taking a deeper dish (smaller f/D) as higher gain. f/D sets the feed angle, not the gain; gain comes from D/λ and η.
Placing the Cassegrain subreflector beyond the focus. The hyperbolic Cassegrain subreflector is inside the focus; the ellipsoidal Gregorian one is beyond it.

quiz.q: Where is the feed of a prime-focus dish, and what does the dish do to the wavefront?
quiz.a: At the focus, f in front of the vertex; the dish turns the spherical wave from the feed into a plane wave across the mouth.

Spillover is feed power that misses the dish (and on receive lets in ground noise); taper loss is gain lost because a feed that lights the rim weakly leaves the outer dish underused. Reducing one raises the other.

quiz.q: A 2 m dish works at 6 GHz with η = 0.55. Find the gain and HPBW.
What diameter gives 45 dBi at 12 GHz with η = 0.65?
Why does a Cassegrain dish suit a low-noise satellite receiver?
quiz.a: The feed and receiver sit behind the vertex, so the line between them is short and low loss, and the feed looks at the cold sky past the subreflector rather than over the rim at the warm ground.

quiz.q: A dish surface has RMS error 2 mm. Compare its loss at 4 GHz and 12 GHz.
quiz.a: At 4 GHz λ = 75 mm, (4π × 2/75)² = 0.112, loss 0.49 dB. At 12 GHz λ = 25 mm, (4π × 2/25)² = 1.011, loss 4.4 dB. The same surface is fine for C band but poor for Ku band.

quiz.q: Moving the feed sideways steers the beam. Why only by a few beamwidths?
quiz.a: An off-focus feed no longer gives an in-phase aperture: the phase error grows with the offset and with D/λ, so the beam broadens, gains a coma lobe and loses gain. Wide scanning needs a moving dish or a phased array.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shaped reflectors bend the paraboloid slightly so that a satellite beam covers a country’s outline. The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune combines thirty 45 m dishes, and very-long-baseline interferometry joins dishes on different continents. Receive systems are judged by G/T, the gain over the system noise temperature, which is why the feed and spillover matter as much as the size. Search for offset reflector, Ruze equation and G/T figure of merit.

figure.caption: The 3 m dish of the worked examples, to scale. Rays from the feed at the focus, 1.2 m in front of the vertex, leave the dish parallel and in phase; the feed must light ±64° to reach the rim of a dish 0.47 m deep. At 4 GHz the 40λ mouth gives 39.8 dBi and a 1.75° beam.
